title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $h=( h_n) $ be a Reiter sequence on $G$ and for a $\tau$-preserving dynamical $(\mathcal{M}, G, \alpha)$, we consider the following averages 
$$ 
A_n^h(x)=:  \int_G \alpha_g(x) h_n(g)~ dm, ~ \text{ for } x \in \cup_{1\leq p < \infty} L^p(M, \tau) \text{ and } n \in \mathbb N.
$$
Then there exists a  subsequence $s=(s_n) $ of $(h_n)$ such that the sequence $(A_n^s)_n$ satisfies the weak type $(1,1)$ inequality and the strong type $(p,p)$ inequality for $p>1$. Furthermore, for every $x \in L^p(M, \tau)$, $A_n^s(x)$ converges in b.a.u. when $1 \leq p< \infty$ and in a.u. when $2 \leq p< \infty$.
head: environment

label: bau conv defn
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{bau conv defn}
A net $\{x_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq L^{0}(\mathcal{M},\tau)$ is said to converge \emph{bilaterally almost uniformly} (b.a.u.) (\textit{resp.} \emph{almost uniformly} (a.u.)) to $x\in L^{0}(\mathcal{M},\tau)$ if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a projection $e \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})$ such that $\tau(1-e) < \varepsilon$ and 
\[
\lim_{i} \|\, e(x_i - x)e \,\| = 0 \quad (\textit{resp. } \lim_{i} \|\, (x_i - x)e \,\| = 0).
\]
head: environment

label: Density_thm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Density_thm}
For every $p \in [1,\infty]$,~~ $L^p(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ is a Banach space with the norm $\|\cdot\|_p$. In particular, $L^2(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ is a Hilbert space with the inner product
\[
\langle x,y\rangle = \tau(y^*x).
\]
Moreover, $\mathcal{M} \cap L^1(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ is dense in $L^p(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ for any $p \in [1,\infty)$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $(x_n)_{n \geq 0}$ be a sequence of positive elements in $L^p(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$. Then $(x_n)_{n \geq 0} \in L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)$ if and only if there exists an element $a \in L^p(\mathcal{M})_+$ such that 
    \[ 
    x_n \leq a \quad \text{for all } n \geq 0. 
    \]
    Furthermore, the norm is given by
    \[ 
    \|(x_n)_{n \geq 0}\|_{L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)} = \inf \big\{ \|a\|_p : a \in L^p(\mathcal{M})_+ \text{ such that } x_n \leq a \text{ for all } n \geq 0 \big\}.
    \]
head: environment

label: strong_pp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{strong_pp}
Let $1 \leq p < \infty$, and let $A = (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of maps on $L^p(\mathcal{M})$. We say that $A$ satisfies a \emph{strong type $(p,p)$ maximal inequality} (or simply the strong $(p,p)$ inequality) if $A$ defines a bounded linear operator from $L^p(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ into the vector-valued space $L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)$. 
Explicitly, this means that there exists a constant $C_p > 0$ such that for every $x \in L^p(\mathcal{M})$, the sequence $(A_n(x))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ belongs to $L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)$ and satisfies
\[
\|(A_n(x))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\|_{L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)} \leq C_p \|x\|_p.
\]

\medskip
\noindent
Equivalently,  for positive elements, 
by the definition of the $L^p(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)$ norm, the sequence of positive maps $A = (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies the strong type $(p,p)$ inequality if and only if there exists a constant $C_p > 0$ such that for every positive element $x \in L^p(\mathcal{M})_+$, one can find a positive element $a \in L^p(\mathcal{M})_+$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $A_n(x) \leq a \quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N}$, and
    \item $\|a\|_p \leq C_p \|x\|_p$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Strong Type $(p,p)$ Inequality

title: Definition
body_md:
Let  \(A = (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence of maps on \(L^1(\mathcal{M})\). We say that \(A\) satisfies the \emph{weak type \((1,1)\) inequality} if \(A\) defines a bounded map from \(L^1(\mathcal{M})\) into \(\Lambda_{1, \infty}(\mathcal{M}; \ell^\infty)\).

\medskip
\noindent
Equivalently, 
for a sequence of maps  $A = (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$  on $L^1(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$,  we say that $A$ satisfies the \emph{weak type $(1,1)$ inequality} if there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for every positive element $x \in L^1(\mathcal{M})_+$ and every $\lambda > 0$, there exists a projection $e \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\tau(1-e) \leq \frac{C}{\lambda} \|x\|_1$, and
    \item $e A_n(x) e \leq \lambda e \quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}

label: sum-maximal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{sum-maximal}
Let $G$ be a locally compact group with a right Haar measure $m$. Suppose $ (f_n)$ and $(h_n) $ are two right Reiter sequences such that  $ c=\displaystyle \sum_{ n=1}^\infty  \left\Vert h_n-f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m) } < \infty $ and suppose that $(A_n^f)$ satisfies the weak type $(1, 1)$ maximal inequality. Then $(A_n^h)$ also satisfies the weak type $(1, 1)$ maximal inequality.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider $ t = \underset{ n \in \mathbb N}{\sup} \left\vert h_n-f_n \right\vert $. Since $ \displaystyle \sum_{ n=1}^\infty  \left\Vert h_n-f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m) } < \infty $, we note that $ t \in L^1(G, m)$. Indeed, it follows that 
\[
t(x)=\sup_n |h_n(x)-f_n(x)|
\leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|h_n(x)-f_n(x)|,
\]
Then by the monotone convergence theorem, we have  
\[
\|t\|_1
\leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|h_n-f_n\|_1<\infty.
\]
Hence, \(t\in L^1(G,m)\).

\medskip
\noindent
Let $ x \in L^1(\mathcal{M}, \tau)_+$, then consider $ a = \int_G \alpha_g(x) t(g) dm$ and it follows that $ a \in L^1(M, \tau)_+$. Let $ w = (h_n-f_n)$, then   we note that 
$$ A^w_n(x) \leq a, ~~ \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb N .$$
Therefore, for given $ \lambda >0$, Consider the projection 
$e = \chi_{[0, \lambda]}(a)$, then note that 
$$ eA_n^w(x)e \leq \lambda e, ~ \text{ for all } n \in  \mathbb N \text{ and } \tau(1-e) \leq \frac{\left\Vertx\right\Vert}{\lambda}.$$
Thus,  the maps $(A_n^w)  $ satisfies weak type $(1, 1)$ maximal inequality.
We note that $ A_n^h = A_n^w +A_n^f$ for all $n \in N$. As both the maps $(A_n^w )$ and  $(A_n^f)$ satisfies the weak type $(1, 1)$  maximal inequality, it follows that $ ( A_n^h)$
also  satisfies the weak type $(1, 1)$ maximal inequality.
head: environment

label: finite-sum-aprox
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We  note that for each $ n \in \mathbb N$, there exists a sequence of  simple positive measurable function $(f_n)$ such that 
 $$ \left\Vert h_n -f_n \right\Vert_{L^1(G,m)} < \varepsilon_n'$$
 where $ \varepsilon_n' = \frac{\varepsilon_n}{4}$.
Now let $ g \in G$, then we observe the following 
\begin{align*}
  \left\Vert \rho_g(f_n) -f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} &=  \left\Vert \rho_g(f_n) -\rho_g(h_n) + \rho_g(h_n) - h_n + h_n -f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} \\
  &= 2 \left\Vert f_n -h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )}  + \left\Vert \rho_g(h_n) -h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} \\
  & \leq \varepsilon_n'  + \left\Vert \rho_g(h_n) -h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} \xrightarrow{ n \to \infty } 0.
\end{align*}
Let $ a_n = \left\Vert f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)}$. 
Then it follows that 
$$ a_n = \left\Vert f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)} = \left\Vert f_n-h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)}+ \left\Vert h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)}\leq \varepsilon_n' + 1.$$
On the other hand, we also have 
\begin{align*}
 &1= \left\Verth_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)} \leq \left\Verth_n-f_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)} + \left\Vertf_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)} \leq a_n + \varepsilon_n'\\
 \implies&  1-\varepsilon_n' \leq a_n. 
\end{align*}
Thus, we have $ 1-\varepsilon_n' \leq a_n \leq 1+\varepsilon_n'.$ Hence,  $ a_n \to 1$ as $ n \to \infty.$ Set $ b_n = a_n^{ -1} \to 1 $ as $n \to \infty$. Now consider 
$$ s_n = b_n f_n.$$
Then note that $ (s_n) $ is Reiter sequence. Suppose there exists a $k \in \mathbb N$ such that $ \varepsilon_n' \leq \frac{1}{k}$, for all $n \in \mathbb N$  and $ k > 1$ and observe that 
$ b_n \leq 2$. Consequently, we obtain the following
\begin{align*}
\left\Vert s_n-h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} &=\left\Vert b_nf_n-h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} \\
&=\left\Vert b_nf_n -b_nh_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m )} + \left\vert1-b_n\right\vert\left\Vert h_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)}\\
&\leq b_n \varepsilon_n' + b_n \left\vert 1-a_n\right\vert \\
&\leq 2 b_n \varepsilon_n' = 4\varepsilon_n'= \varepsilon_n. 
 \end{align*}
This completes the proof.

title: Remark
body_md: We note that Lemma \ref{finite-sum-aprox} holds for a left Reiter sequence under the left Haar measure. Using Theorem \ref{sum-maximal} and Lemma \ref{finite-sum-aprox}, we observe that it is enough to prove the weak type $(1, 1)$ maximal inequality for the maps $(A_n^h)$ associated to the Reiter sequence $(h_n)$ consisting of simple functions.

label: lem: Reiter subsequence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: Reiter subsequence}
Let $(f_n)$ be a right Reiter sequence in $L^1(G, m)$, $(K_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ an increasing sequence of compact sets with $ \underset{n \in \mathbb N}{\cup} K_n= G$ , and $(\varepsilon_n)$ a sequence of positive reals.
                                                              
Then there exists a subsequence $(h_k)$ of $ (f_n)$  such that
\[
\sup_{g \in K_k} \|\rho_g(h_k) - h_k\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon_k, ~~ \text{ for all } k \in \mathbb N.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of a Reiter sequence, for any compact subset $K \subseteq G$, the sequence of translation differences converges to zero uniformly on $K$. That is, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an $N_\varepsilon \in \mathbb{N}$ such that 
\[
\sup_{g \in K} \|\rho_g(f_n) - f_n\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon, ~\text{for all } n \ge N_\varepsilon.
\]
We are given an increasing sequence of compact subsets  $(K_n)$ of $G$ such that $ \cup K_n= G$. We construct the desired subsequence by induction.

\medskip
\noindent
For $k = 1$, corresponding to the compact set $K_1$ and  $\varepsilon_1 >0$, there exists an integer $N_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
\sup_{g \in K_1} \|\rho_g(f_n) - f_n\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon_1 \quad \text{for all } n \ge N_1.
\]
For $k = 2$, corresponding to the compact set $K_2$ and  $\varepsilon_2 > 0$, there exists an integer $N_2 > N_1$ such that
\[
\sup_{g \in K_2} \|\rho_g(f_n) - f_n\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon_2 \quad \text{for all } n \ge N_2.
\]
Proceeding inductively, for any $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we can find an integer $N_k \in \mathbb{N}$ strictly greater than $N_{k-1}$ such that
\[
\sup_{g \in K_k} \|\rho_g(f_n) - f_n\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon_k \quad \text{for all } n \ge N_k.
\]
Let us define a subsequence $(h_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ by setting $h_k = f_{N_k}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Therefore, it follows directly from our construction that
\[
\sup_{g \in K_k} \|\rho_g(h_k) - h_k\|_{ L^1(G, m)} < \varepsilon_k \quad \text{for all } k \in \mathbb{N}.
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: finite-simple
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{finite-simple}
Let $h \in L^1(G, m)$ be a positive simple function with $\|h\|_1=1$, and  $ A \in \mathcal{B}_{ (0, \infty) }$. Then the integral representation over $A$ reduces to a finite sum:
\[
h=     \int_A \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, dt + \int_{A^c} \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, d\mu(t) = \sum_{j=1}^k a_j\frac{ 1_{F_j}}{m(F_j)} + \int_{A^c} \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, d\mu(t),
\]
where $F_t := \{x \in G : h(x) > t\}$, $ E = \{ t>0 : m(F_t) > 0$\},$~\mu$ is a probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ and $\{a_j\}_{j=1}^k \subseteq [0, 1] $ with $ \displaystyle\sum_{ k =1}^n  a_k = \mu(A)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As $F_t := \{x \in G : h(x) > t\}$, we note that 
$$ h = \int_0^\infty 1_{ F_t} ~d t.$$
Since  $h$ is a simple function, it assumes only a finite number of distinct positive values on $G$, which we order as $0 < c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_k$. 
The level set $F_t$ only changes when $t$ crosses one of the values $c_j$. For $t$ between any two adjacent values, the set $F_t$ remains entirely constant. Consequently, the mapping $t \mapsto F_t$ produces only finitely many distinct sets, which we index as $F_1, F_2, \dots, F_k$.
We partition the set $A$ into equivalence classes where the level sets are constant. Define:
\[
    E_j := \{t \in A : F_t = F_j\}.
\]
Since every $t \in (0, \infty)$ corresponds to exactly one set $F_j$, the collection $\{E_j\}_{j=1}^k$ consists of mutually disjoint subsets that fully partition $A$. 
Suppose $ E = \{ t > 0 :  m(F_t) > 0 \}$.
Then using the partition, we decompose the integral over $A$ into a finite sum of integrals:
\begin{align*}
\int_A 1_{ F_t} dt &= \int_A \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)}  m(F_t) 1_E(t)dt\\
&=  \int_A \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, d\mu(t), ~~ \text{ where } 1_E(t) m(F_t) dt = d\mu(t) \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^k \int_{E_j} \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, d\mu(t).
\end{align*}
Now, using Fubini's theorem, we have
\begin{align*}
\mu(0,\infty)=\int_0^\infty m(F_t)dt=\int_0^\infty\int_G 1_{F_t}(x)dm(x)dt
=\int_Gh(x)dm(x)=1.
\end{align*}
For any fixed $j$, the level set $F_t = F_j$ is strictly constant for all $t \in E_j$. This allows us to factor the constant integrand out of each integral:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j=1}^k \int_{E_j} \frac{1_{F_t}}{m(F_t)} \, d\mu(t) &= \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{1_{F_j}}{m(F_j)} \int_{E_j} 1 \, d\mu(t) \\
    &= \sum_{j=1}^k \mu(E_j) \frac{1_{F_j}}{m(F_j)}.
\end{align*}
Take $ a_j = \mu(E_j)$, which satisfies the required conditions.

label: main-thm
title: Theorem

label: error-control
title: Proof
body_md:
First, we fix a compact neighborhood $U$ containing the identity $e$ of $G$ such that $m(U)>0$. Then consider  the $U$-thickening of $K_n$ by
\[
\widetilde K_n:=UK_n.
\]
Since $K_n$ and $U$ are compact, $\widetilde K_n$ is compact, and $m( \widetilde K_n) >0$. 
By Lemma \ref{lem: Reiter subsequence}, we can find a subsequence $ (h_n)$ of $ (s_n)$ 
such that the translation error over these thickened sets satisfies the following; 
\begin{align}\label{error-control}
\sup_{g \in \widetilde{K}_n} \|\rho_{g^{-1}} (h_n) - h_n\|_{L^1(G,m)} \leq \frac{\varepsilon_n}{m( \widetilde{K}_n)}.
\end{align}

\medskip
\noindent
For any $n \in \mathbb N$ and $t > 0$, consider the level sets
\[
    F_{n,t} := \{x \in G : h_n(x) > t\}.
\]
By Fubini's theorem, we have the following layer-cake formulation; 
$$
h_n(x) = \int_0^\infty 1_{F_{n,t}}(x) \, dt.
$$
Since $h_n$ is normalized i.e. $\int_G h_n \, dm = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, integrating over $G$ yields
\[
    \int_0^\infty m(F_{n,t}) \, dt = \int_G h_n(x) \, dm(x) = 1.
\]
We can therefore define a probability measure $\mu_n: \mathcal{B}_{(0, \infty)} \to [0 ,1]$, where $ \mathcal{B}_{(0, \infty)}$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $(0, \infty)$, by $d\mu_n(t) = 1_{ E_n}(t) m(F_{n,t}) \, dt$, where  $E_n = \{t > 0 : m(F_{n,t}) > 0\}$. Then  we can express $h_n$ as an integral convex combination of normalized characteristic functions:
\[
    h_n (x)= \int_0^\infty \frac{1_{F_{n,t}}(x)}{m(F_{n,t})} \, d\mu_n(t), \quad a.e.~~x\in G.
\]

Now, observing that $\rho_{g^{-1}}(h_n)(x)-h_n(x)=\int_0^\infty\big(1_{F_{n,t}g}(x)-1_{F_{n,t}}(x)\big)d\mu_n(t)$, using Fubini's theorem,
\begin{align*}
\left\Vert\rho_{g^{-1}}(h_n)-h_n\right\Vert_1
&= \int_G \left\vert\rho_{g^{-1}}(h_n)(x)-h_n(x)\right\vert \, dm(x) \\
&= \int_0^\infty \int_G \left\vert1_{F_{n,t}g}(x)-1_{F_{n,t}}(x)\right\vert \, dm(x) \, dt \\
&= \int_0^\infty m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t}) \, dt \\
&= \int_0^\infty \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \, d\mu_n(t).
\end{align*}

Integrate this over $g \in \widetilde{K}_n$ with respect to the Haar measure $m$. By Fubini's Theorem, we can swap the order of integration between the Haar measure $m$ and the layer-cake probability measure $\mu_n$. Indeed, we obtain the following 
\begin{align*}
 \int_0^\infty \left( \int_{\widetilde{K}_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} dm(g) \right) d\mu_n(t) 
 &=  \int_{\widetilde{K}_n}  \left(  \int_0^\infty \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} dm(g) \right) d\mu_n(t) \\
 &=    \int_{\widetilde{K}_n}  \left( \|\rho_{g^{-1}} (h_n) - h_n\|_{L^1(G,m)} \right)  dm(g)  \\
 & \leq  \frac{\varepsilon_n}{m( \widetilde{K}_n)}  \cdot m( \widetilde{K}_n)= \varepsilon_n    ~(\text{by Eq.} \ref{error-control}).
\end{align*}
We need to isolate the ``good'' levels. 
Let $\Phi_n(t)$ be the inner integral representing the average symmetric difference for a given level set $F_{n,t}$:
\begin{align}\label{phi-fun}
\Phi_n(t) = \int_{\widetilde{K}_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} dm(g).
\end{align}
Choose a threshold $\delta_n = \sqrt{ \varepsilon_n}$. Now we consider the ``bad'' levels where the average error is too large:
$$B_n = \{t > 0 : \Phi_n(t) > \delta_n\}.$$
By Chebyshev's inequality,  the measure of the bad levels is asymptotically vanishing and good levels converge to $1$; indeed, we note that 
\begin{align}\label{bad-set-control}
\mu_n(B_n) \leq \frac{\varepsilon_n}{\delta_n} = \sqrt{ \varepsilon_n} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 0~ ~\text{ and }  ~~\mu_n(B_n^c) \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} 1.
\end{align}

\noindent Then we  apply Proposition \ref{prop: int over good set} to obtain the following;
\begin{align}\label{Folner-proved}
\sup_{x \in K_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}x \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \leq \frac{2 \delta_n}{m(U)} \lesssim \sqrt{\varepsilon_n}, ~~\text{ for all } t \in B_n^c.
\end{align}
This implies that the level sets $F_{n,t}$ for $t \in B_n^c$ are asymptotically $K_n$-invariant, meaning they form a sequence of F\o lner sets as $n \to \infty$.


\medskip
Finally, we decompose the integral representation of $h_n$ over $B_n^c$ and $B_n$:
\[
    h_n = \int_{B_n^c} \frac{1_{F_{n,t}}}{m(F_{n,t})} \, d\mu_n(t) + \int_{B_n} \frac{1_{F_{n,t}}}{m(F_{n,t})} \, d\mu_n(t).
\]
Suppose $ O_n(g)  =  \int_{B_n} \frac{1_{F_{n,t} } (g)}{m(F_{n,t})} \, d\mu_n(t)$. Note that $ O_n \in L^1(G, m ) $, indeed, we observe that 
$ \left\VertO_n\right\Vert_{ L^1(G, m)}  \leq \mu_n(B_n)  \leq \sqrt{ \varepsilon_n} $ (see Eq.\ref{bad-set-control}).
Moreover, using the Lemma \ref{finite-simple}, we can find a $k_n $ and a set of positive elements $ \{ a_{n, j} : ~ 1 \leq j \leq k_n \} $ such that 
\[
    h_n =  \sum_{ j =1}^{k_n} a_{n, j}  \frac{1_{F_{n,j}}}{m(F_{n,j})}  + O_n.
\]
and $\displaystyle \sum_{j = 1}^{k_n} a_{ n, j}= \mu_n(B_n^c)  \leq 1.$ Furthermore, let $ a_n = \displaystyle \sum_{j = 1}^{k_n} a_{ n, j} $ and it follows that $  a_n \leq 1 $ and $ a_n \xrightarrow{ n \rightarrow \infty } 1$. This completes the proof.

label: rem: Folner cond
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem: Folner cond}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                    
                                                                                                                                                                      
                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
                    
                                                                                        
                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
    Since the group $G$ is assumed to be locally compact second countable, it is $\sigma$-compact and hence it is known that if for some $t\in B_n^c$, and $\varepsilon>0$, there is $n \in \mathbb N$, such that $\frac{m(F_{n,t}g \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \leq \varepsilon$, for all $g \in K$, ($K \subseteq G$ compact), then it is equivalent to the condition that for that particular $t>0$, and for any $\varepsilon>0$ and any compact set $K \subset G$, there is $n \in \mathbb N$ such that $\frac{m(F_{n,t}K \Delta F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \leq \varepsilon$, which will now imply the definition of F\o lner set considered in \cite{cadilhac2025noncommutativemaximalergodicinequalities}.

label: error-control-1
title: Remark
body_md:
We like to highlight that when $G$ is a countable discrete group, then the proof of Theorem \ref{main-thm} is a little less involved. Note that since discrete groups are unimodular, the left and right Haar measures coincide. 
Indeed, establishing the following 
$$
\sup_{g \in K_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \lesssim \sqrt{ \varepsilon_n},
$$
is easier than the continuous case.  But other techniques are similar. Indeed, 
let
 $G$ be a countable discrete group with the counting measure $m$. Suppose 
$(K_n)$ is a increasing sequence of finite  sets in $G$ with  $ \cup_{ n \in \mathbb N} K_n = G$.
Then it is enough  to find a subsequence $ (h_n)$ of $ (s_n)$ 
such that the translation errors over the finite sets $K_n$ satisfy the following; 
\begin{align}\label{error-control-1}
\sup_{g \in {K}_n} \|\rho_{g^{-1}} (h_n) - h_n\|_{L^1(G,m)} \leq \frac{\varepsilon_n}{m( {K}_n)}.
\end{align}
Then we take the function $\Phi_n $ (see the Eq.\ref{phi-fun}) as the following 
\[
    \Phi_n(t) := \sup_{g \in K_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})}.
\]
Now we observe the following; 
\begin{align*}
  \int_0^\infty \Phi_n(t) d\mu_n &= \int_0^\infty \sup_{g \in K_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} d\mu_n \\
  &\leq   \sum_{ g \in K_n} \int_0^\infty  \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} d\mu_n \\
  &=  \sum_{ g \in K_n}\|\rho_{g^{-1}} (h_n) - h_n\|_{L^1(G,m)}   \leq  m( K_n) \frac{\varepsilon_n}{m(K_n)}= \varepsilon_n    ~ (\text{see Eq.} \ref{error-control-1}).
\end{align*}
Thus, this establishes the fact that  $\int_0^\infty \Phi_n(t) \, d\mu_n(t) < \varepsilon_n$.
The rest is similar to what we did in Theorem \ref{main-thm}. Indeed, 
take $\delta_n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_n}$) as in . Define the set of ``bad'' levels by
\[
    B_n := \{t > 0 : \Phi_n(t) > \delta_n\}.
\]
Then deduce that the measure of the bad set vanishes asymptotically:
\[
    \mu_n(B_n) \leq \frac{1}{\delta_n} \int_0^\infty \Phi_n(t) \, d\mu_n(t) \leq \frac{\varepsilon_n}{\delta_n} \to 0.
\]
For the ``good'' levels $B_n^c$, we have $\mu_n(B_n^c) \to 1$. Crucially, for every $t \in B_n^c$, we are guaranteed that
\begin{align*}
\sup_{g \in K_n} \frac{m(F_{n,t}g \mathbin{\Delta} F_{n,t})}{m(F_{n,t})} \leq \delta_n.
\end{align*}
To overcome this difficulty in the continuous setting, we employ the technique of $U$-thickening the given compact sets $(K_n)$ and then proceed with the subsequent analysis (see Proposition \ref{prop: int over good set}).

 Although this represents a necessary topological innovation relative to Namioka's original layer-cake argument \cite{Namioka-1964}, which was inherently restricted to discrete groups and finite sets, the thickening trick is deeply rooted in the study of continuous groups (see \cite{Greenleaf1969} \cite{Emerson1967}).                                                                                                                                               
 This averaging mechanism has long served as the standard bridge between discrete and continuous amenability. By thickening the target sets with a compact neighbourhood of positive Haar measure, we are able to smooth the $L^1$-data, thereby bypassing the measure-theoretic anomalies of uncountably infinite spaces to achieve uniform F\o lner-type invariance.

label: decomposition_of_sequence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{decomposition_of_sequence}
    Let $(s_n)$ be a sequence of non-negative simple functions defined by 
    \[
    s_n = \sum_{j=1}^{k_n} a_{n,j} \frac{\mathbf{1}_{F_{n,j}}}{m(F_{n,j})}. 
    \]
   Suppose $ \sum_{j=1}^{k_n}a_{n,j}=a_n$, then $s_n$ can be rewritten as an infinite sum 
    \[
    s_n = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a'_{n,j} \frac{\mathbf{1}_{F_{n,j}'}}{m(F_{n,j}')},
    \]
    such that the following properties hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item $ F_{n, j}'\in  \{ F_{n, 1 }, F_{n, 2 }, \cdots, F_{n, k_n }\} $ for all $j \in \mathbb N$.
        \item $a'_{n,j} > 0$ for all $j \ge 1$, $\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a'_{n,j}=a_n$ and $ \displaystyle \sum_{ j=1}^\infty  \sqrt{ a_{n, j}'} < \infty  $.
        \item For each fixed $j$, the sequence $(a'_{n,j})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ decreases in $n$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the first row $(n=1)$, which is initially given as $(a_{1,j})_{j=1}^{k_1}$. We define the new infinite sequence of coefficients as follows:
    \[
    a'_{1,j} := 
    \begin{cases} 
        a_{1,j} & \text{for } 1 \leq j \leq k_1 - 1, \\
        \frac{a_{1,k_1}}{2^{j-k_1+1}} & \text{for } j \geq k_1.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    The corresponding new F\o lner sequence sets are defined as:
    \[
    F'_{1,j} := 
    \begin{cases} 
        F_{1,j} & \text{for } 1 \leq j \leq k_1, \\
        F_{1, k_1} & \text{for } j \geq k_1 + 1.
    \end{cases}
    \]
Next, we construct the second row $(n=2)$. If $a_{2,j} \leq a'_{1,j}$ for all $j$, we define the new second row exactly as we did for the first row. Otherwise, we proceed by redistributing the weights. Let $1 \leq i \leq k_2$ be the first index such that $a_{2,j} \leq a'_{1,j}$ for $1 \leq j \leq i$, but $a_{2,i+1} > a'_{1,i+1}$. We begin modifying the sequence by setting:
    \[
    a''_{2,j} := 
    \begin{cases} 
        a_{2,j} & \text{for } 1 \leq j \leq i, \\
        a'_{1,i+1} & \text{for } j = i+1.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    For the next term, we evaluate the remainder $a_{2,i+1} - a'_{1,i+1}$. If this remainder is less than or equal to $a'_{1,i+2}$, we set:
    \[
    a''_{2,i+2} := a_{2,i+1} - a'_{1,i+1}. 
    \]
    Otherwise, we cap it by setting $a''_{2,i+2} := a'_{1,i+2}$, and consider the new remainder $a_{2,i+1} - a'_{1,i+1} - a'_{1,i+2}$. We repeat this shifting process until the remaining part becomes strictly smaller than the corresponding $a'_{1,j}$. This process clearly ends in finitely many steps. 
    
\medskip

    Suppose that the process for $a_{2,i+1}$ terminates at the index $i'$. We then move to the next term from the second row, $a_{2,i+2}$, and continue the same redistribution process starting against $a'_{1, i'+1}$. Since there are only finitely many terms in the original second row, this entire redistribution concludes after a finite number of steps. Note that the terms generated at each step are strictly positive. 

    \medskip
    \noindent
    Let the final non-zero term obtained in this process be $a''_{2,j'}$ at some index $j'$. If $j' < k_1$, we replace $a''_{2,j'}$ by $\frac{a''_{2,j'}}{2}$ and continue the infinite halving process. Thus, without loss of generality, we may assume $j' \geq k_1$. We can now formally define the infinite sequence for the second row as:
    \[
    a'_{2,j} := 
    \begin{cases} 
        a''_{2,j} & \text{if } j < j', \\
        \frac{a''_{2,j'}}{2^{j-j'+1}} & \text{if } j \geq j'.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    By construction, this ensures that $0 < a'_{2,j} \leq a'_{1,j}$ for all $j$, and that $\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a'_{2,j}=a_2$. Moreover, define $ F_{n, j}'$ as the first row in the tail part, and in between we keep the same $F_{2, j} $ with the decompositions of $ a_{2, j}$ to obtain the following: 
$$  \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a'_{n,j} \frac{\mathbf{1}_{F_{n,j}'}}{m(F_{n,j}',)} =  \sum_{j=1}^{k_n} a_{n,j} \frac{\mathbf{1}_{F_{n,j}}}{m(F_{n,j})} $$

    \medskip
    For the general inductive step, given the $n$-th row $(a'_{n,j})_{j=1}^{\infty}$, we can construct the $(n+1)$-th row $(a'_{n+1,j})_{j=1}^{\infty}$ using the exact same redistribution argument. This guarantees that $0 < a'_{n+1,j} \leq a'_{n,j}$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a'_{n+1,j}=a_{n+1}$, which completes the proof.

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{Filtered F\o lner sequence} is a triple $\mathcal{S}:=((F_n)_n, (B_n)_n, (\mathcal{P}_n)_n)$, where $(F_n)_n$ is a F\o lner sequence of subsets of $G$, $(B_n)_n$ is a sequence of compact subsets of $G$ and $(\mathcal{P}_n)_n$ is a sequence of partitions of the group $G$, satisfying the following conditions:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item for any $n \in \mathbb N$, and $A \in \mathcal{P}_n$, there exists $\gamma \in G$ such that $A \subseteq \gamma B_n$,
        \item for any $n \geq k$, the set $F_n$ is $(2^{n-k}, B_k)$- boundary invariant.
    \end{enumerate}
    Now an atom $A \in \mathcal{P}_k$ is said to be \emph{admissible} if for all $n < k$, the set $A$ is $(2^{n-k}, F_n)$-invariant (that is, $\left\vertAF_n \setminus A\right\vert \leq 2^{n-k} \left\vertF_n\right\vert$ and $\left\vertAF_n^{-1} \setminus A\right\vert \leq 2^{n-k} \left\vertF_n\right\vert$). Let $\mathcal{P}_n^a$ denotes the collection of admissible atoms of $\mathcal{P}_n$ and define
    $$Adm(\mathcal{S}):= \cap_{n\geq 0} \cup_{A \in \mathcal{P}_n^a} A.$$
    \noindent Let $0<c<1$, we say that $\mathcal{S}$ is $c$-\emph{admissible} if $\underline{B}(Adm(\mathcal{S})) \geq 1-c$. By a slight abuse of notation, we say that a F\o lner sequence of sets $(F_n)_n$ of $G$ is called \emph{admissible} if there exists a triple $\mathcal{S}:=((F_n)_n, (B_n)_n, (\mathcal{P}_n)_n)$ and $c \in (0,1)$ satisfying the above conditions.

label: weak_type_(1,1)_ergodic
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since ${A}_{n,j}^s(x)=\frac{1}{m(F_{n,j})}\int_{F_{n,j}}\alpha_g(x)dm(g)$ and for all $j,$ $(F_{n,j})$ is an admissible F\o lner sequence, by \cite{cadilhac2022noncommutative} ${A}_{n,j}^s(x)$ satisfies weak type $(1,1)$ maximal inequality. Hence, there exist $C'>0$ (independent of the F\o lner sequences) and $e_{j,x} \in \mathcal{M}$ with
    
    $$e_{j,x}{A}_{n,j}^s(x)e_{j,x} \leq \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{a_{1,j}}}\cdot \frac{1}{\big(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^\infty \sqrt{a_{1,j}}\big)} \text{ and } \tau(1-e_{j,x}) \leq C'\frac{\|x\|_1\cdot \sqrt{a_{1,j}}}{\lambda}\sum_{j=1}^\infty \sqrt{a_{1,j}}.$$
    
    Let us define $e_x:= \displaystyle\bigwedge_je_{j,x}.$
    Hence, $$\tau(1-e_x) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\tau(1-e_{j,x}) \leq C'\frac{\|x\|_1}{\lambda}\big(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{a_{1,j}}\big)^2 \leq C\frac{\|x\|_1}{\lambda} $$
where $C=C'\cdot \big(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{a_{1,j}}\big)^2.$ Now from the Lemma \ref{decomposition_of_sequence} we note that $a_{n,j} \leq a_{1,j}$ for all $j\in \mathbb N.$ Therefore, we have 
\begin{align*}
    e_x{A}_{n}(x)e_x&=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_{n,j}e_x{A}_{n,j}(x)e_x \\
    &\leq \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_{n,j}e_{j,x}{A}_{n,j}(x)e_{j,x}\\
    &\leq \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_{1,j}e_{j,x}{A}_{n,j}(x)e_{j,x}\\
    &\leq \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_{1,j} \big(\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{a_{1,j}}}\big)\cdot \frac{1}{\big(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{a_{1,j}}\big)}=\lambda.
\end{align*}

Note that since for all $n \in \mathbb N$, $\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} a_{n,j} =a_n$ and $(a_n)_n$ is a bounded sequence, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \left\Vert{A}^s(x)\right\Vert_\infty \lesssim \left\Vertx\right\Vert_\infty, \text{ for all } x \in \mathcal{M},
\end{align*}
which by definition implies that the sequence $(A^s_n)_n$ is weak type $(\infty, \infty)$. Therefore, by \cite[Theorem 1.3]{cadilhac2025revisiting}, we show that $( A^s_n)_n$ satisfies strong $(p,p)$.

label: WW_theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{WW_theorem}
Let $G$ be a l.c.s.c group with a two-sided Reiter sequence acting continuously on a finite von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ with finite trace $\tau.$ Suppose that $x\in L^p(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ and $(\pi, \phi, u)$ is as above. Then ${A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}(x)$ converges in b.a.u. uniformly over the symbol $(\pi, \phi, u).$ Moreover, if $x$ is in the weak-mixing part of the representation of $\alpha$, then the average converges to $0$ in b.a.u.

Let $ \mathcal{M}$ be a finite von Neumann algebra with a f.n trace $\tau$ and $ (\mathcal{M}, G, \alpha) $ be a $\tau$-preserving non-commutative dynamical system. Then $\mathcal{M}$ can be written as

label: vand_corput
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: van der Corput inequality along a Reiter sequence

label: A
title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by evaluating the following,
\begin{align*}
    \bigg\|\int_G f(g)s_n(g)dm(g)-&\int_G\int_Gf(gh)s_n(g)s_k(h)dm(g)dm(h)\bigg\| \\
    &\leq \bigg\|\int_G \int_G f(g)s_n(g)s_k(h)dm(g)dm(h)-\int_G\int_Gf(g)s_n(gh^{-1})s_k(h)dm(g)dm(h)\bigg\|\\
    &\leq \bigg\|\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(g)s_n(g)s_k(h)dm(g) - \int_G f(g)s_n(gh^{-1})s_k(h)dm(g)\bigg)dm(h)\bigg\|\\
   &\leq \int_G\int_G \|f\|_\infty s_k(h)|s_n(g) - s_n(gh^{-1})|dm(g)dm(h)\\
   &= \|f\|_\infty\int_G  \|s_n-\rho_{h^{-1}} (s_n)\|_1s_k(h)dm(h).
\end{align*}
Therefore, we obtain 
\begin{align}\label{A}
    \bigg\|\int_G f(g)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg\|^2 \leq \bigg\|\int_G\int_G&f(gh)s_n(g)s_k(h)dm(g)dm(h)\bigg\|^2+ 2\|f\|_\infty^2\int_G  \|s_n-\rho_{h^{-1}} (s_n)\|_1s_k(h)dm(h)\nonumber\\
    &+ \|f\|_\infty^2 \Bigg(\int_G  \|s_n-\rho_{h^{-1}} (s_n)\|_1s_k(h)dm(h)\Bigg)^2.
\end{align}
We now estimate the first term separately, 
\begin{align*}
&\bigg\|\int_G\int_Gf(gh)s_n(g)s_k(h)dm(g)dm(h)\bigg\|^2 \\
  = & \bigg\|\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(gh)s_k(h)dm(h)\bigg)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg\|^2 \\
  &\leq \bigg\|\int_G \bigg|\int_Gf(gh)s_k(h)dm(h) \bigg|^2s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg\|\\
&\leq\bigg\|\int_G\int_G\int_Gf(gh_1)^*f(gh_2)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg\|\\
&=\bigg\|\int_G\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(gh_1)^*f(gh_2)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\bigg\|\\
&=\bigg\|\int_G\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(g)^*f(gh_1^{-1}h_2)s_n(gh_1^{-1})dm(g)\bigg)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\bigg\|\\
&\leq\bigg\|\int_G\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(g)^*f(gh_1^{-1}h_2)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\bigg\|\\
&\qquad + \|f\|_{\infty}^2\int_G\|s_n-\rho_{h_1^{-1}}(s_n)\|s_k(h_1)dm(h_1). 
\end{align*}
Hence, the lemma follows from Ineq. \ref{A} and the above estimate.

label: simplification

body_md:
\label{simplification}
    Since $\mathcal{M}\cap L^2(\mathcal{M},\tau)$ is dense in $L^p(\mathcal{M},\tau)$ for all $1<p\leq \infty,$ by Theorem \ref{Banach_Principle} it suffices to prove the b.a.u. convergence of ${A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}$ for $x \in L^2(\mathcal{M}, \tau).$ Using the JdLG decomposition (Theorem \ref{JdLG}), we will prove this convergence separately for $x \in L^2(\mathcal{M},\tau)_c$ and $x \in \mathcal{M}_{wm}$, which will complete the proof of Theorem \ref{WW_theorem}. Since $\mathcal{U}_d$ is a compact group, the Stone-Weierstrass theorem allows us to approximate $\phi$ uniformly by matrix coefficients, that is the functions of the form $u\in \mathcal{U}_d \mapsto \langle u\xi,\eta\rangle,~~\xi,\eta \in \mathbb C^d.$ Therefore, to prove convergence, it suffices to assume that $\phi$ is of this form.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $x\in L^2(\mathcal{M},\tau)_c$ and $\xi, \eta \in \mathbb C.$ Then the following weighted average 
   $$B_n(x)= \int_G\alpha_g(x)\langle \pi(g)u\xi,\eta \rangle s_n(g)dm(g)$$ converges in a.u.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In  view of \cite[Theorem 15.14]{Eisner2015} and Theorem \ref{Banach_Principle}, it suffices to prove the convergence of $B_n(x)$ for $x$ from finite dimensional $G-$ invariant subspace of $L^2(\mathcal{M}, \tau).$ Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a finite dimensional invariant subspace of $L^2(\mathcal{M}, \tau)$ with an orthonormal basis $\{x_1,\cdots, x_m\}.$ Then we have 
$$\alpha_g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m \langle\alpha_g(x),x_i\rangle x_i$$
Now 
\begin{align*}
    B_n(x)&=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_G\langle\alpha_g(x),x_i
\rangle \langle\pi(g)u\xi,\eta \rangle s_n(g)dm(g) x_i\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_G\bigg\langle\alpha_g(x)\otimes \pi(g)u\xi,x_i\otimes \eta\bigg\rangle  s_n(g)dm(g) x_i\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigg\langle\int_G\alpha_g(x)\otimes \pi(g)u\xi ~s_n(g) dm(g), x_i\otimes \eta \bigg\rangle  x_i.
\end{align*}
Applying the Mean Ergodic Theorem for Reiter sequence yields
$$\int_G\alpha_g(x)\otimes \pi(g)u\xi ~s_n(g) dm(g)= \int_G(\alpha_g\otimes \pi(g))(x\otimes u\xi)s_n(g)dm(g)$$
converges. Therefore, since there are finitely many $x_i$ we can find a single projection $e \in \mathcal{M}$ with arbitrarily small trace of its complement such that $\mathbb{B}_n(x)e$ converges.

label: keylemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $G$ be a l.c.s.c group with two-sided Reiter sequence $(s_n)$ and $\mathcal{M}$ be a finite von Neumann algebra with f.n trace $\tau.$ Suppose $(\mathcal{M},G, \alpha)$ is as before. Let $x\in \mathcal{M}_{wm}.$ Then ${A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}(x)$ converges to $0$ in a.u. uniformly in symbols $(\pi,\phi,u).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of Remark \ref{simplification}, we can take the weighted average as
$${A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}(x)= \int_G\alpha_g(x)\langle \pi(g)u\xi,\eta \rangle s_n(g)dm(g), ~~\xi,\eta \in \mathbb C^d.$$
Since $G$ is second countable, there exists a countable dense subset $\{g_i\}_{i \in \mathbb N}$ of $G.$
Let $\varepsilon >0.$ Applying Proposition \ref{ergodic_L2} there exist projections $e_i \in \mathcal{M}$ with $\tau(1-e_i) <\frac{\varepsilon}{2^i}$ and 
$$A^s_n(x^*\alpha_{g_i}(x))e_i \to \tau(x^*\alpha_{g_i}(x))e_i \text{ in } \|\cdot\|_{\infty}.$$ Define $e:=\displaystyle \bigwedge_{i\in \mathbb N} e_i.$ Therefore $$A^h_n(x^*\alpha_{g_i}(x))e \to \tau(x^*\alpha_{g_i}(x))e \text{ in } \|\cdot\|_{\infty} \text{ and } \tau(1-e) < \varepsilon.$$
Since the action $\alpha$ is continuous and $\{g_i\}_{i\in \mathbb N}$ is dense in $G$, it follows that 
\begin{align*}
    A^h_n(x^*\alpha_{g}(x))e \to \tau(x^*\alpha_{g}(x))e \text{ in } \|\cdot\|_{\infty} \text{ for all } g \in G.
\end{align*}
Consider the function $f:G \to \mathcal{M} \otimes M_d(\mathbb C),$ defined by $f(g):= \alpha_g(x)e\otimes \pi(g)u,~~u\in \mathcal{U}_d.$ So, $f$ is bounded under $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ of $\mathcal{M} \otimes M_d(\mathbb C).$ Next we will use the Lemma \ref{vand_corput}. Since $(s_n)_n$ is a two-sided Reiter sequence and $s_k\in L^1(G)$, by the dominated convergence theorem the last two terms on the R.H.S of Ineq. \ref{vand_cor_inequality} converge to $0$. Hence, it suffices to prove that the first term on the R.H.S of Ineq. \ref{vand_cor_inequality} converges to $0$. We have
$$f(g)^*f(gh_1^{-1}h_2)=e\alpha_g(x^*\alpha_{h_1^{-1}h_2}(x))e\otimes u^*\pi(h_1^{-1}h_2)u.$$
Therefore, computing the first term of the R.H.S of Ineq. \ref{vand_cor_inequality} we obtain
\begin{align*}
\bigg\|&\int_G\int_G\bigg(\int_Gf(g)^*f(gh_1^{-1}h_2)s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\bigg\|\\
&=\bigg\|\int_G\int_G\bigg(\int_Ge\alpha_g(x^*\alpha_{h_1^{-1}h_2}(x))e\otimes u^*\pi(h_1^{-1}h_2)u~s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg)s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\bigg\|\\
&=\int_G\int_G\bigg\|\int_Ge\alpha_g(x^*\alpha_{h_1^{-1}h_2}(x))e\otimes u^*\pi(h_1^{-1}h_2)u~s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg\|s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\\
&\leq \int_G\int_G\bigg\|{A}^s_n(x^*\alpha_{h_1^{-1}h_2}(x))\bigg\|s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2)\\
&= \int_G\int_G\big|\tau(x^*\alpha_{h_1^{-1}h_2}(x))\big|s_k(h_1)s_k(h_2)dm(h_1)dm(h_2).
\end{align*}
Hence, using Lemma \ref{keylemma} we obtain
$$ \int_G\big(\alpha_g(x)e \otimes \pi(g)u\big) ~s_n(g)dm(g) \longrightarrow 0$$ in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ of the von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}\otimes M_d(\mathbb C).$ Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
    {A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}(x)e&= \int_G\alpha_g(x)e\langle \pi(g)u\xi,\eta \rangle s_n(g)dm(g)\\
    &=\int_Gid_{\mathcal{M}}\otimes\omega_{\xi,\eta}(\alpha_g(x)e\otimes \pi(g)u)~s_n(g)dm(g)\\
    &=id_{\mathcal{M}}\otimes\omega_{\xi,\eta} \bigg(\int_G\big(\alpha_g(x)e \otimes \pi(g)u\big) ~s_n(g)dm(g)\bigg),
\end{align*}
where $\omega_{\xi,\eta}:\mathcal{U}_d \to \mathbb C$ defined as $\omega_{\xi,\eta}(u):= \langle u\xi,\eta\rangle.$ Since $id_{\mathcal{M}}\otimes \omega_{\xi,\eta}$ is a bounded operator, we conclude that ${A}_n^{\pi,\phi,u}(x)e \longrightarrow 0$ in $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ of $\mathcal{M}.$
